summary: Round 2: physical-digital food ideas for college students, hostile judges also rule on a social/competition layer, survivors rebuilt and executed
logs: 14 ideas in the pool (including 2 seeded from round 1)
3 survived with at most 1 kill vote; advancing 3

all_ideas_scored.name: Cleaned Out (the plate is the ballot box)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: A dorm cook-off where nobody votes: whichever dish gets eaten fastest wins, and every chef pays the pot in proportion to the food left on their plate.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: The social layer is the core here, so it helps rather than hurts. With no rival plates there is no game at all. A season table for the floor (the 'Floor 4 Dumpling League') ranks chefs by wins and money won. A short feed post goes up after each cook-off ('Maya's potstickers cleared in 11:42, a personal record'). The Strava-like part is a chef's personal best clear time, which only means something because other people ate the food. This is competitive cooking, not a health or diet score.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: live 7 social=helps - Strongest survivor. I found no app, Devpost project or HCI paper that turns how much is left on a plate into a ballot that moves money. The 'emptiest dish wins' rule exists only as an office and potluck folk custom judged by eye, with no software and no money. The judge's own bite moves a stranger's pending charge, so the judge is the actor within 10 seconds, and it passes the Friday-night test because cook-offs already happen. Risks: (a) Traycer (2026 winner), Winnow and Leanpath mean 'camera measures what's left on a plate' is not new, so open on the ballot and the money, not the vision; (b) 'losers pay for leftovers' needs a friendly frame, for example the pot buys next round's ingredients; (c) only countable foods work. It also absorbs #7 Bean Vote, which is the weaker version of the same cook-off. | social: Rival plates ARE the game, and the money comes from co-present competitors, so competition is load-bearing. A floor season table ('Floor 4 Dumpling League') and personal-best clear times give it repeat value. A cross-campus Strava feed would add nothing for judges and should stay out of the pitch.

cynical-student: live 6 social=helps - The best judge moment in the set that doesn't need a phone: the judge eats a cookie and somebody else's charge drops. Nobody fills out a ballot, so there's no homework. The weak spot is the student. Am I putting $10 down to cook for my floor and then paying for whatever nobody ate? Maybe once, at a Friendsgiving cook-off that already has an entry fee. The plate nearest the door wins, and a chef can eat their own plate. It's kept alive by the demo, not by my weekend. Pitch it as a cook-off buy-in where the winner takes the pot, which floors already do, and lead with 'eating is the vote.' Don't lead with 'you pay for your leftovers,' because that line punishes the people who did the work. | social: Rival plates in the same room are the whole game. The 'Floor 4 Dumpling League' season table is borderline. A personal-best clear time is fine because other people's eating sets it. Cut the feed posts, since nobody follows a dumpling account.

expo-judge: live 8 social=helps - Best table of the batch. In the first 10 seconds I'm the actor: I eat a cookie and someone else's pending charge drops on screen. The money is a punchline caused by a physical act, the way Minty's was. Counting cookies on three fixed plates is exactly what Perceptron does well, and four people can build it in 36 hours. Every Visa primitive has a visible job (hold, live partial-capture preview, void for the winner, partial capture for losers, push to the winner), and none is mocked. It is not Math Sandbox, because the food itself is the input. Two things I'd push on. First, 'losers pay into a pot that goes to the winner' is an entry-fee prize pool, and a Visa person will hear it that way. Reframe the pot as 'losers reimburse the winner's ingredients' (capture capped at the winner's declared grocery cost) or deliver it only as the capped ingredient mandate, and the gambling optics go away. Second, the self-eating exploit needs a one-line answer (for example, chefs are tagged and the camera ignores bites from tagged chefs, or just call it a strategy). Fold Bean Vote's kind framing ('your leftovers reimburse the cook who won') into this one and drop Bean Vote. | social: Rival plates are the game, and the people eating are the voters, so social is load-bearing, not decoration. Keep the floor league and the personal-best clear time. Drop any feed beyond one post-round clip. A season table of 'money won' pushes it back toward a betting pool.

all_ideas_scored.name: Bite Bounty
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: "I'll Venmo you $5 if you eat that," but enforced: friends put holds on their cards to back a food dare, the camera referees, and you get paid for every second you hold out.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Social is the core, and here it clearly makes the idea better, because the money has to come from someone else and the fun needs an audience. A dare goes to the group chat, friends join the pot by placing holds, and the clip plus payout gets posted to a friends feed. Strava-style 'segments' are set per food (longest anyone held a Warhead Extreme, fastest to finish a raw lemon) with a leaderboard for each. There is no global score across foods, since a single number would turn it into an endurance grind.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=helps - The core interaction (friends lock money behind a dare, proof releases it) is old and crowded. Per-second partial capture and a live referee are a real twist, but the idea's own write-up admits it is 'Bounty narrowed to food dares', and Bounty won in 2026. Default kill. Separately, an endurance food dare is the One Chip Challenge's lineage (pulled in 2023 after a teen died). A Visa judge will flinch at a payment brand sponsoring 'suffer longer, earn more', even with sour candy. | social: The money must come from backers and the fun needs an audience, so social is load-bearing. Per-food segment leaderboards are the most Strava-native idea in the set. That doesn't save it, because the core is prior art.

cynical-student: live 8 social=helps - This passes the Friday-night test without effort: 'twenty bucks if you eat that' already happens in every dorm. It fixes the two ways those dares really fail. Backers say 'I was joking,' and holds stop that. People argue over 'you spat it out,' and the camera settles it. Paying by the second makes the judge's own suffering the price, a Minty-grade punchline, and the hand-on-milk trigger is easy for vision to catch. The challenger never puts money in, so it's sponsorship, not wagering. Hard rules: only sour, weird, or first-try foods (Warheads, lemon, natto, durian candy), never extreme capsaicin, because of the One Chip Challenge death. Expect 'Bounty again' and answer with per-second capture plus live refereeing. Also offer judges a second dare item, in case one won't eat candy. | social: Money has to come from friends and the fun needs an audience, so social is required. Per-food Strava-style segments ('longest Warhead Extreme hold') are the one competition layer in this set that works: a physical act sets the record and people would screenshot it. Keep the no-global-score rule.

expo-judge: live 7 social=helps - Strong Minty shape: I suffer through a Warhead, my own face sets the price, and the moment I grab the milk the ticker freezes and holds void. The judge is the actor and the punchline is physical. Settling by partial capture in proportion to seconds survived, with the rest voided, is a fresh live use of real primitives, and the challenger never puts money in, so it is sponsorship, not a wager. The vision that matters (hand touches glass) is easy. Label OCR is mostly a gimmick, and spit detection is shaky, so make 'touched the milk' the only fail condition in the demo. Risks: Bounty (2026 winner) is escrow-on-proof, so lead with the per-second ticker, not escrow. Dares-for-money carries safety optics after the One Chip Challenge death, so whitelist sour and weird foods only and say so out loud. Borrow #6's routing as an option (the pot pays for the group's food or a club fundraiser) to soften the 'paying people to hurt themselves' read. | social: The money has to come from friends and the fun needs an audience, so social is the engine. Per-food 'segments' (longest Warhead hold among your friends) are the one Strava idea in this batch that works, but keep them within a friend group. A global endurance leaderboard turns into a health-optics problem.

all_ideas_scored.name: Toppled (snack Jenga where the tower is the bill)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: At a party, everyone stacks the host's snacks into one tower. A camera prices the tower live as it grows, and whoever knocks it over pays the host for every snack in the pile. Then everyone eats the wreckage.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: The game is social by nature and has no solo version, so the social layer isn't optional. The answer to the team's question for this idea: do NOT add a Strava-style feed or a cross-group leaderboard. Ranking strangers' snack towers adds nothing, and a 'who pays most' ranking turns a party bit into a shame chart. The one extra worth adding is a replay wall of the tallest tower and the most expensive collapse, which people share as clips. That is where the virality comes from, not from points.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: live 5 social=neutral - Survives on a technicality. Loser-pays Jenga exists only as a house rule, and automated credit card roulette exists (PigeonPayer), but I found no build where the grocery pieces are OCR-priced live and the physical collapse settles a capped hold. It has the most slapstick money moment in the set, and the judge balances a real snack. It loses points for three reasons: (1) gambling optics, since a Visa judge hears 'credit card roulette' no matter how the skill defense is framed; (2) attributing who toppled the tower needs turn order, so the vision does less than claimed; (3) the payment mapping is one capture and N voids, the least interesting Visa story among the survivors. Keep it as a backup, not the lead. | social: The game is co-present by nature. A replay wall of the most expensive collapse is shareable, but persistent 'who pays most' standings would be a shame chart. A Strava feed adds nothing.

cynical-student: KILL 5 social=helps - Same game as #1, so ship one. Uneven snacks (Takis bags, Pringles tubes) make 'is it placed' and 'did it collapse' fuzzy, and working out who toppled it from 'the hand in frame' is fragile in a crowd. #1's identical cans are more reliable, and its 'placing a can lowers your share' rule is better design than 'tower value equals the snacks.' Take the one good idea here, labels read to price the tower live, and fold it into #1 if the team wants a stronger grocery tie. | social: The replay wall of collapses is the right viral layer and should carry into #1.

expo-judge: live 7 social=helps - I place a Takis bag on a wobbling tower, the 'tower value' climbs from label OCR prices, it crashes, and a slow-motion replay is stamped 'TOPPLED: $18.69, Judge'. That's touchable, understood in 10 seconds, and the money is the slapstick punchline. Collapse detection is easy (structure height collapses), and turn order handles attribution, so drop the hand-in-frame claim. Visa is real and bounded: a $20 cap hold per player, partial capture for the toppler, voids for everyone else, a push to the host. The cap is the trust line: 'the worst a collapse can cost you is what you approved'. Risks: 'loser pays' gambling optics (defend it as loser-buys-the-snacks with no pot and no winner payout), and the time to rebuild the tower between judges (pre-build a half tower and keep a can-based fallback from #1). Pick this over #1 because the snacks are both the game pieces and the bill, which makes it a grocery idea. | social: No solo version exists, so the people in the room are the product. The replay wall (most expensive collapse) is the right persistent layer because it's shareable and has no points. A cross-group 'who paid most' ranking would hurt.

all_ideas_scored.name: Toppler (the can tower holds the bill)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: Stack LaCroix cans into a tower to decide who pays for the pizza. Every can you place moves a dollar of your share onto the tower, and whoever knocks it over pays everything that's on it.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Competition is the game itself. The persistent layer is light and on purpose: a friend group's long-running standings ('Jake has paid for 6 of 9 pizzas') and a record tower height, so the fun stays at the table rather than in a feed. A full Strava-style feed would add nothing here, since the point is the moment with friends, not a profile.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=neutral - A duplicate of #9 with a weaker prop. Empty cans are generic blocks, which makes this a Jenga drinking game with a payment attached, while #9 at least makes the pieces themselves the priced groceries. 'Loser pays the bill' is credit card roulette, which a Stripe team automated with card capture back in 2014. The same gambling optics that killed Fridge Futures apply. If the team wants the tower mechanic, keep #9 and drop this one. | social: The game is inherently multiplayer, but persistent standings ('Jake paid for 6 of 9') become a shame chart and add nothing to the demo.

cynical-student: live 7 social=helps - I would tell my roommate about this tonight: 'Jenga with the empty LaCroix cans, and whoever knocks it over pays for the pizza.' It's already a Friday-night ritual (credit card roulette, Jenga drinking games), and the props are already trash on the table. The push-your-luck rule is real game design: placing a can lowers your own share but raises the pot for everyone. Identical cans make it the most reliable vision demo here. Counting is trivial and the collapse is unmistakable. One crash triggers void, partial capture, and capture at once, the cleanest 'one physical event, three Visa outcomes' shot. Risk: a Visa judge says gambling. Defense: no house, no payout to winners, the loser covers food everyone eats, the cap bounds the loss, and it takes skill. Merge in #9's label-read pricing if the team wants it closer to groceries. | social: Competition at the table is the product. A light friend-group ledger ('Jake has paid for 6 of 9 pizzas') and a record tower height are the right size. A feed or a cross-group leaderboard would add nothing.

expo-judge: KILL 6 social=neutral - This is the same mechanic as #9 (a tower that holds the bill, and the toppler pays), with worse domain fit. Empty cans are a party prop, not groceries. The 'each can moves $1 of your share onto the tower' math is clever push-your-luck design, but I can't follow it in 90 seconds while also stacking. Cans do reset faster at an expo than snacks do, so borrow cans for the demo reset if #9's snack tower turns out too slow to rebuild. Kill as a duplicate. | social: In-room competition is the game. The long-running 'Jake paid 6 of 9 pizzas' standings is a mild shame chart, and it adds nothing a judge sees.

all_ideas_scored.name: Locked Ten (the grocery date challenge, but the card enforces the rules)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: Two people each get a $10 card that stays locked until the camera confirms their basket meets the dare, like one item for each letter of their date's name. Then it unlocks for exactly $10 for 10 minutes, and you check out.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Two-player head-to-head by design (date or best friend), with a group mode for floor events ('$7 Chopped Run': teams get locked cards with a mystery rule, then cook what they bought). A small leaderboard for the floor-event mode (fastest unlock, most under budget) makes that mode better. For dates, any public leaderboard makes it worse. The social output there is the reveal (swap bags) and a single shareable card ('Locked Ten: SAM, $9.41, 6:12 left'), which is TikTok-native already. No in-app feed.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=neutral - The game works on the honor system and the idea admits 'why do I need the app?' is a thin defense. The money moment is a permission flip (LOCKED to LIVE), not a punchline where money moves as a consequence. Checkout needs a sandbox terminal standing in for a real store register, which hostile judges read as mocked. Lock-and-unlock cards exist in teen and parent fintech (Greenlight, BusyKid). A mini shelf with OCR'd labels and a checklist of chips also reads as the 'grocery list card' pattern the team is trying to escape. I could not confirm the exact name-letter variant online, but the Dollar Tree date-night challenge format is well documented. | social: Two-player head-to-head is the game. A floor 'Chopped Run' leaderboard helps that mode a little, and any public layer hurts the date mode. On balance it doesn't change the verdict.

cynical-student: KILL 5 social=neutral - The ritual is real (TikTok $10 grocery date), and OCR letter-matching on labels shows Perceptron well. But would I install an app to lock my own debit card for a date game I can play on the honor system? No. The money moment is spending your own $10 at a register, while the strongest ideas move someone else's money. The sandbox-terminal checkout is also the part judges will smell as mocked. It's a nice feature for RAs, not a product. | social: Shareable reveal cards are fine, but that's TikTok doing the work. The floor 'Chopped Run' leaderboard is an RA event, not something students start themselves.

expo-judge: live 6 social=neutral - Answers the Listcard question correctly: a physical game state unlocks a card, but through real token suspend/resume plus a $10 mandate whose expiry is the challenge clock. Nothing is enforced at the item level, so nothing is mocked. As a Visa person, this is the most native trust story on the floor: the card is dead until you earn it, then it can't overspend or outlive the timer. Weaknesses: holding items up to a phone one by one feels like a barcode scanner, not a spectacle. The money moment (the card flips to LIVE) is satisfying but not funny. And 'people already play this without an app' is a real hit. It survives as the Visa-judge backup pick, not the overall-prize pick. Make the unlock louder (a full-screen card flip with a countdown, then a tap to a sandbox terminal), and lead with the group 'Chopped Run' mode for the creativity score. | social: Head-to-head is built in. A floor-event leaderboard helps a little in group mode, but for dates any public board hurts. The shareable result card is the right amount.

all_ideas_scored.name: Enryo (the last-dumpling auction)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: When one dumpling is left on the shared plate and nobody will take it, hovering your chopsticks over it is a live bid, and whoever holds out longest pays for it.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: The competition is the auction itself. The persistent layer is purely for laughs: a record-price board ('Most ever paid for one gyoza: $6.25, Anson') and a monthly 'Most Polite' badge for the friend who never bids. Anything more serious, like a ranking of who eats the most, would push it toward the dead pay-per-slice idea and should stay out.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: live 5 social=neutral - Survives the prior-art hunt but is thin. I found no app, game or Devpost project where hovering chopsticks are a live bid on the last piece. Bid-as-hold is standard charity-auction plumbing, so the only novelty is the physical paddle, and that is exactly the part that has to work. Concerns: chopstick-tip tracking at expo lighting is the riskiest vision task in the set; it sits next to the dead pay-per-slice family; it is a one-per-night bit. Best used as a 20-second closer inside #0 (the last cookie on the winning plate goes to auction), not as the whole project. | social: The auction needs people in the room, but that is the mechanic itself, not a social layer. A record-price board is a joke that judges won't weigh. Any 'who eats most' ranking would drag it into pay-per-slice.

cynical-student: KILL 4 social=neutral - The name is lovely and the bit is cute, but no 20-year-old pays a friend $1.75 for a gyoza. You split it or someone grabs it. It's a once-a-night joke with no reason to open the app, and a hostile judge files it straight into the dead 'camera prices who ate what from a shared plate' family. Tracking two pairs of hovering chopstick tips under expo lighting is also the shakiest vision dependency in the set. | social: The auction is social by nature, but a record-price board and a 'Most Polite' badge are padding. No social layer saves a mechanic people won't trigger.

expo-judge: KILL 5 social=neutral - A genuinely funny 20-second bit, and the chopstick paddles are the most physical way to do the last-item auction. But tracking chopstick tips hovering over one gyoza under expo lighting is the kind of thing that fails on the third judge. The whole interaction is one item and one moment. A hostile judge will file it under 'camera at a shared plate charging for food', the family round 1 killed. The idea has no staying power, as the pitch itself admits. Use it as a closer mode inside another idea, not as a project. | social: The auction needs people in the room, but the record-price board is a one-time joke. No persistent layer would help.

all_ideas_scored.name: Pledge Plate (walkathon pledges, but for eating contests)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: Friends pledge a set amount per wing, dumpling or hot chip that you get down. The camera counts, and their card holds turn into real charges while everyone watches.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Native and essential, but kept local. The pledgers are the audience, and the reason to eat one more wing is hearing your friends' phones go off. The pledge board ('Maya: $0.50/wing, cap $6') is the trash talk. Ruling for the team: a room-level live board makes it better. A global or Strava-style leaderboard of eating counts makes it worse (it turns into competitive overeating, and judges will raise health concerns). Keep it to the room plus one shareable 10-second clip with the final count and total raised.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=helps - Per-wing pledges for eating contests already run on real platforms. 99Pledges hosts the Big Wing Challenge with per-wing pledge pages, and Givebutter hosts wing challenges with sponsor minimums. The only addition is the camera count driving partial capture. The idea's own write-up says a judge will call it '99Pledges with a camera', and that is the kill. The Visa mapping is the cleanest in the set (the pledge IS an authorization), and that mechanic is worth lifting into a survivor. Competitive overeating also invites health objections. | social: Pledgers in the room are the audience, and the phones buzzing is the hook, so the in-room board is good. A global eating-count leaderboard is clearly harmful (overeating and health optics).

cynical-student: KILL 4 social=neutral - Honestly it's '99Pledges with a camera,' and eating-volume contests carry health optics Visa judges will flag. The Oreo-stacking expo version is a cookie-counting demo, not a feat. The good part, friends' money moving with your body, is done better by Bite Bounty, where endurance replaces volume. Fold per-unit pledging into Bite Bounty as an optional mode. | social: A room-level pledge board is fine and a global eating leaderboard is toxic. The team already said both. Neither fixes the derivative core.

expo-judge: KILL 6 social=helps - The cleanest Visa mapping in the set: the pledge literally is a capped hold, with capture equal to count times rate and the rest voided. But the expo version stacks Oreos instead of eating, which breaks the conceit, and 'walkathon with a camera' sticks after one sentence. It also does the same job as #3 (friends sponsor your feat, holds fill live), with a weaker prop and less face-on-the-line comedy. Kill as a separate project and merge its per-unit mode and its fundraiser/'pledges buy the food' routing into Bite Bounty. | social: The board in the room and the friends' phones buzzing are the reason to eat one more. Its own ruling is correct: a global eating-count leaderboard would hurt because of competitive-overeating optics.

all_ideas_scored.name: Bean Vote (the potluck where votes pay the cooks back)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: At a cook-off or potluck, every guest's entry fee is a card hold. Guests drop jelly beans in a cup in front of the dishes they love, and the camera counts the beans to decide how much of each cook's grocery bill gets paid back.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Yes, and it makes the idea better, but at the floor or club level, not globally. Within a party: a live 'payback bar' per cook on the TV. Across a season: a floor or club 'kitchen standings' page that shows each cook's lifetime payback rate (what percentage of their grocery spend friends voted back) across monthly cook-offs. That gives recurring dorm and club cook-offs a reason to come back. A Strava-style public feed would make it worse: food rankings among strangers are noise, and the stakes only matter among people who tasted the food.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=helps - Beans or tickets in jars for People's Choice is a standard cook-off format, and a BBQ forum has already proposed splitting taste-ticket money to cooks by ticket count, which is this exact payout mechanic without the camera. Counting beans in cups is the least interesting vision task here, and a counter of physical tokens on a table drifts toward Math Sandbox territory. It is strictly dominated by #0, where eating is the vote and no extra token is needed. Merge the 'pay back the cook, never overcharge' framing into #0. | social: A floor or club 'kitchen standings' table across monthly cook-offs is a reasonable retention story. It just belongs to #0.

cynical-student: KILL 4 social=neutral - Wholesome but sleepy. Paying $5 to drop a jelly bean so my friend gets reimbursed for groceries is a voting app plus Splitwise. It's utility over a solved problem, round 1's lesson #1. Cleaned Out gets the same cook-off energy with a better moment, because eating is the vote and there's no bean step. If the team wants a cook-off, keep #0's mechanic and borrow #7's 'cap at what the cook spent.' | social: 'Lifetime payback rate' standings make cooking a stat. They don't hurt much, but nobody will open them.

expo-judge: KILL 5 social=helps - The kinder sibling of #0, and the kindness is its best feature (nobody is charged extra; votes reimburse cooks). But it adds a step: taste, then find a bean, then drop it. Counting colored beans piled inside paper cups is an occlusion problem a fixed overhead camera will get wrong. And 'voting app plus Splitwise' is the obvious kill line. In #0, eating is the vote, so it removes the ballot entirely. Kill, and take its 'reimburse up to declared grocery cost, never overpay' cap into #0 to fix that idea's prize-pool optics. | social: Club or floor kitchen standings would bring people back to recurring cook-offs, and limiting it to people who tasted the food is right. But the same layer works better on #0.

all_ideas_scored.name: Potluck Bouncer
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: RSVP to the Friendsgiving potluck with a $10 hold. A camera at the door checks what you brought: homemade gets your hold voided, a bag of Tostitos costs $3, and showing up empty-handed costs the full $10, all going to the host's turkey fund.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Kept to the party. A 'spread board' on the TV shows each guest's contribution, the host fund, and a light-hearted Hall of Shame for chip-bringers. No leaderboard across parties or for hosts. A ranking would reward hosts who set punitive deposits, and the social pressure only works within one friend group.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 4 social=hurts - At its core this is a commitment deposit forfeited on failure (Snitch, 2026 winner) with a vision referee. Charging a friend $3 for bringing chips to your own party fails the cynical-student test: hosts won't put deposits on friends, and guests would find it hostile. Label OCR on a Tostitos bag is easy and unremarkable. The 'penalties buy the missing drinks' agent step is the one fresh beat, but it is a small agent feature by the brief's own rules. It also overlaps heavily with #11. | social: A 'Hall of Shame for chip-bringers' is public penalty in a friend group. It makes the idea feel punitive rather than fun, and judges will say so.

cynical-student: KILL 3 social=hurts - Charging my friends a deposit to come to my Friendsgiving, then having a camera roast their Tostitos, is how you end up with no friends. Nobody would set this up unprompted. Store-bought versus homemade detection is also flaky: foil covers everything, and Costco trays get re-plated. It's Snitch with a bouncer skin. | social: A Hall of Shame for chip-bringers is public shaming at a party you're hosting. Visibility here works as pressure, not fun.

expo-judge: KILL 4 social=hurts - It's a commitment deposit with a vision referee, sitting right next to Snitch. Grading homemade versus store-bought is mean-spirited and trivially gamed: a foil-covered tray can hold anything, including the Tostitos. Friends charging friends a deposit to attend Friendsgiving fails the cynical-student test. Here the agent buying missing drinks is a third gimmick on top of the other two. The Visa mapping (void, partial capture, full capture at expiry) is clean, but the core social premise is hostile. | social: A Hall of Shame for chip-bringers is exactly the shame chart a judge will call toxic. The social pressure is coercion, not fun.

all_ideas_scored.name: Table Stakes (bring something or it's bought for you)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: RSVPing to a potluck places a small hold on your card. Put a dish in an open spot on the host's table and the camera releases your hold live on the TV. If you show up empty-handed, your hold buys what's missing.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: The social pressure IS the mechanism: the TV board shows who brought what in real time, and that public visibility is why people bring things. Here, more social is not better. A cross-party leaderboard or a 'flaker score' would be toxic, and judges would say so. The right amount is the live table board for the night, plus a 'dish of the night' vote that gives nothing but bragging rights. This is the idea where the team should state openly that it deliberately keeps the social layer small.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 3 social=hurts - The idea's own write-up calls it the most utility-like and the most exposed to round-1's 'friction removal over a solved problem' kill, and I agree. Stake-and-verify-proof is Snitch and Bounty (both 2026 winners). Potluck coordination is Partiful and SignUpGenius. Taped zones on a table with a camera recognizing what's placed in each zone is the closest thing in the set to a Math Sandbox tabletop reskin. Attributing a dish to a guest by 'arrival order and hand in frame' is fragile. A duplicate of #5. | social: Visible who-brought-what boards are pressure, not fun, and the write-up concedes a flaker score would be toxic.

cynical-student: KILL 3 social=hurts - A deposit to attend a friend's party, again. The team admits it's the least whimsical and most utility-shaped. Working out which guest placed which dish is the hardest vision problem in the set, it's Snitch plus Bounty in setting and mechanic, and the agent buying LaCroix is filler. | social: The public who-brought-what board is a pressure mechanism, and pressure at a friend's party is cringe.

expo-judge: KILL 5 social=hurts - The most useful idea and the least whimsical, which is exactly the round-1 'utility over a solved problem' kill. Mechanically it's Snitch or Bounty stake-and-verify with a table as the proof. Working out which guest set down which bag from arrival order and the hand in frame will misattribute at a busy expo. The money moment (a hold dissolves) is relief, not a punchline. A deposit to attend a friend's party reads as passive-aggressive. Partiful already covers chip-ins. Duplicate of #5's space. | social: Public who-brought-what pressure is the mechanism. That's social as enforcement, and any extension (a flaker score) is toxic. Even the small version makes the party feel policed.

all_ideas_scored.name: Sink Surge
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: Every dirty dish in the shared sink has a bounty that rises by the hour like Uber surge pricing, paid by the whole house, and whoever finally washes it gets the money.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Kept to the house, and that helps. A house board shows live prices on every dish in the sink (the shared joke is watching the pan go up), and a monthly earnings board shows things like 'Maya made $23 off the sink.' There is no leaderboard between houses or campus-wide. Comparing houses adds nothing, and naming who left dishes would bring back the petty blame version.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 3 social=neutral - A camera on a dorm sink is one of the most-built hackathon and maker projects there is, and DishWatcher on Devpost already tracks dishes left and cleaned with alerts and a leaderboard. Judges will say 'I've seen the dish camera' before the surge price lands. Paid chores is also a solved category (Chorsee, BusyKid, Greenlight). It fails the cynical-student test too: nobody sets up dish bounties on a Friday night, and racking a ketchup plate is a chore, not a conceit. | social: A house-only earnings board is fine but adds nothing a judge would score, and anything wider brings back roommate shaming.

cynical-student: KILL 3 social=hurts - A camera aimed at my sink, so my roommates can pay me to do chores, is a parent, a landlord, and surveillance in one. It's also trivially gamed: dirty a plate, let it surge, wash it, collect. It's dishes, not food, so it barely fits the domain. Judges have seen a dozen dish-shaming cameras, and 'no blame' doesn't change what the hardware is. | social: Even a house-only earnings board ('Maya made $23 off the sink') turns into a running tally of who does housework, which is the fight it claims to remove.

expo-judge: KILL 4 social=neutral - I'm going to see a dish camera at another table today, and surge pricing doesn't change that first impression. Asking me to wipe ketchup off a plate into a plastic tub at an expo is a weak prop. Tracking a dish from sink to water to rack reliably is harder than it looks. A permanent camera over a shared sink is a privacy ask most houses refuse. And it's a chore app, not food or groceries. Incremental auth is real, but the house-splits-the-bounty mechanic is Splitwise for chores. The cynical student wouldn't set this up. | social: Limiting it to the house is right, but an earnings board for dishes doesn't create any pull. It's a chore ledger.

all_ideas_scored.name: Last Dibs (the last one goes to auction)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: When the camera sees only one donut, slice, or dumpling left in the shared box, that last one goes up for a 15-second live auction among everyone in the room. The winner pays whoever bought the box.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: The live auction among people in the same room is the social layer. It only works face to face, which is the strongest argument that social can make an idea better: here, the social layer is the product. Recommended extra: a 'Last Dibs Hall of Fame' (most ever paid for a last slice, most generous box-buyer earnings), which is cheap, funny, and screenshot-able. Not recommended: a Strava-style feed, because no one cares about another dorm's donut auctions.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 3 social=neutral - A duplicate of #2 with the physical interaction removed. Bids happen on phones, so the camera only triggers a phone auction with bid holds, which every charity-auction platform already runs. That leaves 'the camera counted to one', a weak use of vision and squarely in the 'pizza camera again' family that died in round 1 (Per Slice, Bites). If the auction survives at all, it is as Enryo's chopstick version folded into another idea. | social: A room-only auction is the mechanic, not a layer, and a Hall of Fame is a screenshot gag that judges won't score.

cynical-student: KILL 3 social=neutral - It's Enryo with the physical part removed: you bid on your phone. People won't pay $3 out of pride for one donut more than once. The camera only counts to 1, so the vision is decoration. 'Pizza camera again' kills it with judges. | social: An in-room auction is social, but the Hall of Fame is filler on a bit that doesn't last.

expo-judge: KILL 4 social=neutral - The camera only notices that the count hit 1. Everything after that is a phone auction app with judges tapping bid buttons, which is the chat-style screen interaction I'm trying to escape today. The bid-as-auth with reversal on outbid is a nice auth-churn demo, and the 'Visa asked if you're sure about the $6 donut' step-up is a good line. But the physical-digital link is thin and it's the same setting as the killed pay-per-slice ideas. If anything from this survives, it's the step-up prompt joke, and it belongs in another idea. | social: A live auction in the room is social by nature, but the Hall of Fame is a novelty that doesn't make me care at the table.

all_ideas_scored.name: House Board (round-1 survivor, rebuilt)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: The whiteboard on your shared fridge is the house card: write an item and the house card can buy it, erase it and the card stops, anyone can erase but only funders can add.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: House members see who added what; optional house leaderboard of who stocks the most.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 2 social=hurts - Breaks two hard rules in the brief. Its money moment ('the card declines eggs') is an item-level decline, which is mocked and banned. Handwriting on a surface read by a camera is the Math Sandbox pattern. Shared house cards and shared lists are solved (Ysplit, Privacy.com, OurGroceries), and whiteboard-to-grocery-list OCR is published academic work. It is also a friction-removal utility, the failure mode the round-1 executioner named. | social: A 'who stocks the most' house leaderboard turns a shared-utility tool into a scorekeeping chore and invites resentment.

cynical-student: KILL 2 social=hurts - It depends on item-level allowlist declines, which the brief says are mocked. It's a utility over solved list apps, and a whiteboard and marker is close enough to Math Sandbox to draw the comparison. | social: A leaderboard of who stocks the most is exactly the 'leaderboard nobody asked for.'

expo-judge: KILL 3 social=hurts - The money moment is 'the runner's card declines eggs in the store', which is an item-level decline at a register. That is mocked and I'll see through it. The shared-card-for-housemates premise is plumbing (Privacy.com, Ysplit), and a fridge whiteboard as a control surface is the paper-as-input pattern that reads as Math Sandbox and Listcard again. The optional 'who stocks most' leaderboard is the dead Strava-for-fridge idea. | social: A who-stocks-most house leaderboard is the already-killed fridge-points idea and adds blame to a utility.

all_ideas_scored.name: Reach-In (round-1 survivor, rebuilt)
all_ideas_scored.one_liner: Tap the Takis in your friend's camera at Trader Joe's; a hold lands on your card, and the runner's card limit climbs only when your item hits their basket.
all_ideas_scored.social_layer: Watching friends' 20-second aisle windows in the group feed.
verdicts: prior-art-hunter: KILL 2 social=neutral - This is the dead 'grab me something from TJ's' errand run, which the brief bans in any form (Kando Errands, Buy4Me, GrocerMate, NeedAnything exist). The runner card's climbing limit relies on issuing a just-in-time card to a friend, which is mocked and banned. Round 1 already flagged this exact weakness: the most interesting part is the most mocked. | social: Watching friends' aisle windows in a feed is a utility side panel. Nobody would browse it for fun, so it neither rescues nor sinks the idea.

cynical-student: KILL 1 social=hurts - It's the 'grab me something from TJ's' errand run, which is dead in any form, and the run card is admittedly mocked. | social: Watching friends' aisle clips in a feed is content nobody wants.

expo-judge: KILL 3 social=neutral - This is the dead 'grab me something from TJ's' errand run, and issuing the run card is mocked by its own admission. The core loop is utility (remote shopping), not a physical event causing a fun money consequence. TikTok Shop and Verishop already did tap-in-a-live-stream. | social: Watching friends' aisle clips in a feed is content nobody asked for. It doesn't save an idea that's already dead.

general_social_takes.take:
Ruling: a social layer helps only when it is in the room and supplies the money. It should be rivals or an audience who are physically present and whose own holds get captured or voided by what the camera sees. In #0 Cleaned Out, the rival plates and the guests eating are the whole game, so competition is load-bearing. In #3 Bite Bounty and #6 Pledge Plate the backers in the room are the hook, but both died on prior art.

A persistent Strava layer (feed, cross-group leaderboard, global goal score, personal-best profile) hurts or does nothing, for four reasons. (1) Judges have about 3 minutes at the table and can't experience a feed. (2) Any single 'goal score' slides into the dead health or lifestyle-score family. (3) Rankings of who pays, flakes, eats most or leaves dishes become shame charts (#5, #11, #12 all got worse from their social layers). (4) The 20-year-old does the cook-off or dare for the night, not for a profile.

The one form that works: a live, in-room scoreboard where the bars are other people's pending holds draining in real time, plus at most a small floor or club season table (for example 'Floor 4 Dumpling League' wins and pot) mentioned in one sentence as the retention story. Don't build a feed.

On the hostile-agent question: they go after social layers that are bolted on (a feed slapped onto a utility) or that rank people. They leave alone social layers where removing the other players removes the game.

Prior-art summary: only #0 (lead, 7), #9 (backup, 5) and #2 (fold in as a closer for #0, 5) survive. #1, #10, #7 and #11 die as duplicates of stronger siblings. #3 (Bounty, Double Dog, Monster Dare), #4 (DishWatcher, Dirty Dish Detector), #6 (99Pledges Big Wing Challenge) and #5 (Snitch) die because the core interaction already exists. #12 and #13 break the brief's banned-mock rules.

On physical-digital intersection: the survivors work because the food itself is the controller (eaten cookies, a toppling snack tower, chopsticks), not paper or cards read by a camera. Grocery list cards, whiteboards and taped table zones (#8, #11, #12) are the Math Sandbox echo and should be dropped.

A social layer helps only when it is the table itself: people in the same room whose money moves because of something physical one of them just did. That's why Bite Bounty, Toppler and Cleaned Out survive. The friends backing you, the next player's can, and the rival plate are the mechanic, not features added on top. Anything persistent and abstract hurts: Strava-style feeds, campus or cross-group leaderboards, lifestyle-style 'goal scores', and halls of shame. A cynical student reads those as homework or surveillance, and judges have seen dozens. Deposits to attend a friend's party (Potluck Bouncer, Table Stakes) are the worst version, because social pressure turns into a bill. Chores (Sink Surge) fail too, because the score is a tally of who does housework. The one form of competition that works is a record set by a physical act, on a single specific challenge, kept within your friend group and shareable as a clip: 'longest anyone held a Warhead Extreme,' 'tallest can tower before it fell,' 'fastest plate cleared.' Each is a Strava segment, not a Strava profile. There's no global score and no point system across activities. On 'what would the hostile agents go after': in every survivor, the goal score must be something your body or hands did at the table, never a measure of how well you live. On the physical-digital question: the props should be the food and its trash (candy, cans, plates), with the camera as referee and Visa holds as the scoreboard. Never paper and a projector, because that's Math Sandbox. Recommended build order: Bite Bounty first, with the safety allowlist and per-food records. Toppler is the backup or second mode, with #9's label pricing folded in. Cleaned Out is a stretch if the cook-off framing tests well.

Ruling: a social layer helps only when it's live, in the room, and the other people are the source of the money or the stakes. Their holds are what's at risk, their bites are the votes, their turn might be the one that topples the tower. Every survivor (Cleaned Out, Toppled, Bite Bounty) fails without other people physically present, and that's why they work. A persistent Strava-style feed, a cross-group or campus leaderboard, or a single 'goal score' makes every idea worse, for four reasons. (1) A judge sees it as bolted-on gamification in a 3-minute visit. (2) The hostile reads write themselves: a 'who paid most' ranking is a shame chart, cross-group eating counts are health optics, and money-won tables turn a game into a betting pool. (3) It's the already-killed Strava-for-fridge and goal-adherence family. (4) Nobody cares about another dorm's donut auction. The one form that works is the round's live screen plus a single shareable replay clip stamped with the money (for example 'TOPPLED: $18.69, Judge Chen' or 'Warhead held 22s, $8.80'). Optionally add one friend-group-scoped record (personal-best clear time, longest hold) and nothing more. Any 'goal' belongs inside the round as a timer or cap, never as a score that follows a person around. The Visa angle that makes these social games acceptable is the cap. Every player pre-approves an amount-capped hold, so 'the most this can cost you is what you approved' is the trust story. Lead with it to pre-empt the gambling objection on anything shaped like loser-pays or a pot. Structure money as reimbursing someone's groceries or covering shared food, never as winnings.

rebuilt.name: Cleaned Out: Loser Buys the Groceries
rebuilt.pitch_10s: A cook-off where nobody votes. Eat a cookie, and that chef's bill drops on the screen. When the timer ends, whatever is left on the losers' plates pays for the winner's groceries, and the winner never makes more than they spent.
rebuilt.the_new_thing: The serving plate acts as the ballot box and also as the meter on a real Visa authorization. Each chef's $10 hold is shown live as $10 times the share of their plate still full, so every bite a guest takes visibly lowers that chef's possible charge. There are no ballots, ratings or QR codes: eating is the vote. Two changes from the survivor fix the judges' objections. (1) It is now 'loser buys the groceries' and no longer an entry-fee prize pool. I borrowed Bean Vote's cap mechanic: the winner is paid back only their declared ingredient cost, the losers' captures are scaled to fit under that cap, and the rest of every hold is voided. Nobody makes a profit, so a Visa reviewer cannot read it as a betting pool. (2) The camera has a fairness rule. Chefs wear a bright 'chef band' wristband. If a banded hand takes an item from any plate, Perceptron grounds the hand at the plate when the count drops, and that item still counts as left over: 'CHEF HAND, doesn't count.' This turns the self-eating exploit into a second funny beat in the demo. Plates are told apart by color (red, blue, green), not by position or name tents, so they can be moved during a round and the plate nearest the door has no lasting edge. Plates are also paper-free, so nobody can say 'Math Sandbox again'. Prior plate-waste cameras (Winnow, Leanpath, Traycer) measure waste in kitchens. None of them uses how fast a plate empties as a live ballot that sets a partial capture.
rebuilt.physical_prop: Three colored plates (red, blue, green), each starting with 12 cookies in a different flavor (chocolate chip, snickerdoodle, matcha). Each plate's chef is a teammate wearing a neon chef-band wristband. A phone on a gooseneck clamp looks straight down at the table. A TV shows three draining money bars. A big physical arcade button ends the round, and the judge presses it. A bag of spare cookies sits under the table to restock between judges.
rebuilt.core_loop: 1) Registration (30 s per chef on the phone): pick a plate color, authorize a $10 amount-capped hold, and declare your ingredient cost (capped at $10, and shown to everyone, so lying is a social risk). 2) Put the plates out and start a 20 to 45 minute timer. Guests do nothing except eat. 3) Perceptron counts the items on each colored plate about once a second. The count is smoothed with a median over three frames, only updates when no hand is over the plate, and can never go up unless a chef hand caused the drop. Each chef's live meter is $10 times the fraction left, and the leaderboard reorders as people eat. 4) When the timer ends, the emptiest plate wins and its chef's hold is voided. Each loser's 'leftover amount' is scaled down so the total equals the winner's declared ingredient cost, that amount is partially captured, and the rest of every hold is voided. The winner is paid by Visa Direct push-to-card. 5) A settlement receipt shows the overhead snapshot of each plate at close as evidence. The floor league updates wins and personal-best clear times. Next week, the winner defends the title.
rebuilt.demo_script_90s: 0-10s: The judge walks up to three plates that are partly eaten from earlier visitors (red 7 left, blue 6 left, green 9 left). The TV shows RED $5.83, BLUE $5.00, GREEN $7.50, and blue is in second. Teammate: 'Nobody votes here. Eating is the vote. Try the blue one.' 10-20s: The judge eats a blue snickerdoodle. Within about a second, the blue bar drains from $5.00 to $4.17 and blue jumps to first with a little 'your bite moved $0.83' toast. 20-35s: Teammate: 'Your leftovers are your bill. Whatever's still on your plate at the end pays for the winner's groceries.' The green chef, wearing a wristband, sneaks a cookie off his own plate. The screen flashes 'CHEF HAND, doesn't count' and green stays at 9 / $7.50. The judge laughs. 35-50s: Teammate: 'These are real Visa sandbox holds. Each chef authorized $10, and that number is the most they can ever lose.' The judge presses the arcade button. 50-70s: Settlement plays out bar by bar. BLUE wins, and its $10 hold shows VOIDED. Blue declared $9.00 in ingredients, so the losers' leftover amounts ($5.83 + $7.50 = $13.33) are scaled to fit $9.00. RED is partially captured at $3.94 with $6.06 released. GREEN is partially captured at $5.06 with $4.94 released. Blue's phone buzzes: 'Visa Direct: +$9.00. Your groceries are paid for.' 70-90s: We show the overhead snapshot attached to the receipt and the Floor 4 Cookie League table (wins, personal-best clear time 11:42). Teammate: 'The winner never profits, losers never pay more than their leftovers, and guests never pay anything. It's loser buys the groceries, settled by the plates themselves.' We restock the plates for the next judge.
rebuilt.money_moment: There are two beats. First, the judge's own bite lowers a stranger's pending charge by $0.83 on screen and reorders the leaderboard. That is a physical act with a visible money result, the same move as Minty's toothbrush. Second, the judge presses the button and settlement happens all at once: the winner's hold is VOIDED, the losers are partially captured at $3.94 and $5.06 (scaled exactly to the winner's $9.00 grocery cost), the unused hold is released on screen, and a push-to-card lands on the winner's phone. The punchline line is now 'loser buys the groceries.' Everyone already knows that bet, unlike the old 'you pay for what nobody wanted,' which punished the people who cooked.
rebuilt.social_layer_decision: KEEP the core competition, TRIM the league, CUT the feed. All three judges ruled that social helps here, and the reason matters for the team's general question. Competition helps when the rivals are in the same room and are where the money comes from. A Strava-style async feed hurts because it is decoration that nobody follows. So: (1) Keep: rival plates in one room are the game. With no rival there is nothing to settle. (2) Keep: a personal-best clear time ('Maya's potstickers cleared in 11:42'), since other people's eating sets it and you can't game it alone. (3) Trim: the Floor 4 league table ranks only wins and clear times, never money won, following the expo judge's warning that a money leaderboard turns it back into a betting pool. In the pitch it gets one screen and five seconds, as the reason people come back. (4) Cut: feed posts, cross-campus rankings and followers, as the cynical student said ('nobody follows a dumpling account'). The one share item is an optional 10-second timelapse clip of the winning plate emptying, for the group chat. Answer for the team: a social layer is worth adding only when the other people are physically part of the mechanic. A goal score or feed added on top of a solo action is what round 1 already killed.
rebuilt.visa_role: Every primitive has a visible job and runs in sandbox, with nothing mocked. (1) Authorization: each chef places a $10 amount-capped authorization at registration (Cybersource / Visa Acceptance sandbox auth), which is their published maximum loss. (2) Live partial-capture preview: the app recomputes each hold's possible capture from the plate count and draws it as the draining bar. (3) Void: at close, the winner's hold is fully reversed. (4) Partial capture: each loser is captured for min($10 × fraction left, their share of the winner's declared ingredient cost). The total is capped at that cost, so no one profits. (5) Release: the rest of each loser's hold is reversed, and the screen shows the released amount. (6) Payout: the winner gets the captured total through Visa Direct push-to-card (an OCT in sandbox). Optional stretch feature, kept out of the main demo: the winner can take the payout as a Payment Instructions mandate capped at that amount with a 7-day expiry, ingredients only, and an agent spends it on next round's groceries through Trusted Agent Protocol signed checkout. That makes 'loser buys the groceries' literal. It is a small feature and never the core. Pitch line to a Visa judge: 'This is a split payment whose split comes from what people physically ate. Auth, partial capture, void and push are all doing real work.'
rebuilt.trust_story: Guests never pay or sign up. They only eat. A chef's worst case is $10 and is shown before they authorize. The winner can only be paid back declared ingredient cost (capped at $10, shown to everyone), so there is no profit motive and no prize pool, which fixes the gambling-optics objection. Fairness: a bite taken by a chef-band hand still counts as left over. Plates are recognized by color, so they can be moved or reshuffled at halftime to cancel out position advantage. The count can only go down, and only when no hand is over the plate, so you can't fake it by holding a cookie up. Evidence: the settlement receipt includes the overhead snapshot and the count history for each plate, which ends the 'who actually won' argument and serves as the record for any dispute. Before capture, any chef can hit 'contest' and the host confirms the count from the snapshot. Privacy: the camera stores counts and plate crops only. No faces are kept, and hands are detected only by wristband color. Honest limits we say out loud: it only works for countable foods (cookies, dumplings, wings, sushi, slices), and a guest who grabs five cookies at once counts as five votes. That is real demand, and we treat it as part of the game.
rebuilt.build_36h: Person A, vision (hours 0-30): a fixed overhead phone camera; the host taps three plate circles once to set regions, and plates are tracked by color so they can move. Perceptron counts the items in each region at 1-2 Hz. Smoothing: a three-frame median, count can only go down, and no update while a hand is over the plate. Chef band: detect the neon wristband near a plate at the moment its count drops, and roll back that drop. A hidden hotkey lets a person override counts if Perceptron struggles during a judge visit. Test on 20 minutes of real cookie-eating video by hour 12. Person B, Visa (hours 0-24): Cybersource sandbox auth for $10, partial capture, and reversal/void; Visa Direct sandbox OCT push; the settlement math (scale to the winner's cap, round to the cent, put the remainder on the largest loser); idempotent settlement so pressing the button twice is safe. Person C, big-screen UI (hours 4-32): three draining bars, an animated leaderboard reorder, the 'your bite moved $X' toast, the 'CHEF HAND' flash, the settlement sequence (VOIDED / CAPTURED / RELEASED / push-to-card), and the receipt with snapshots. Person D, chef app and glue (hours 0-36): registration (color, hold, ingredient cost), winner push notification, a league table (wins and personal-best clear time only), the USB arcade button mapped to end-of-round, a restock/reset flow for consecutive judges, and preparing the props. Stretch only if everything else is solid by hour 30: the PI mandate plus TAP agent buying next round's ingredients. Cut first if time runs short: the league table becomes a static screen.
rebuilt.fatal_flaw: None fatal; every objection now has an answer. The biggest remaining risks: (1) Repeat use. The cynical student was honest that a student would do this at a Friendsgiving or floor cook-off that already exists, not every week. We pitch it as the stakes and the settlement layer for cook-offs that already happen, not as a habit app, and accept that this caps 'daily active' claims. (2) Counting robustness at the expo table: hands, napkins and crumbs over plates. We handle it by updating only when no hand is in the region and keeping a hidden manual override, and we must test with real eaters before the event. (3) Declared ingredient cost is on the honor system. Showing it to everyone and capping it at $10 limits the damage, but a picky Visa judge may poke at it. Answer: the worst a lie can do is cost $10, everyone sees it, and the floor deals with it socially.

rebuilt.name: Sour Clock (renamed from Bite Bounty so judges don't hear "Bounty again" before they've seen anything)
rebuilt.pitch_10s: "Twenty bucks if you eat that," except your friends' cards are already on the hook. Hold a Warhead in your mouth and their holds drain onto your card every second. The moment you lift the milk, the clock freezes and the rest goes back to them.
rebuilt.the_new_thing:
A dare where the price is set by time, on a live meter, with two sides watching one camera. Every escrow-on-proof app (Bounty, Double Dog, Monster Dare, CrowdDare) is a yes/no: post proof, release funds. In Sour Clock the hold moves while the dare is happening. The challenger watches their number climb, and each backer watches their own hold drain on their phone, so the backers are rooting for you to quit and you're fighting to last. That two-sided live tension is the product. The escrow is only the plumbing that makes it binding.

Fixes from the judges' objections:
(1) There is one fail condition and it's easy to see: the milk glass leaves its marked coaster zone. That's position tracking, not "did a hand brush it". Spit detection is cut from the demo and stays only as a backer-flagged replay.
(2) Label OCR now has a real job: it's the safety gate. Perceptron reads the package and its ingredient panel before the clock can start. Only whitelisted sour, bitter or weird items unlock (Warheads Extreme, Toxic Waste, lemon wedge, natto, salmiakki, durian candy). Any label mentioning capsaicin, ghost pepper, Carolina Reaper or "challenge chip" refuses to open a dare. It also checks the ingredient list against the allergens the challenger declared at signup.
(3) A hard 30-second clock. Reaching 30 seconds is "beating the Sour Clock" and caps the payout, so this is never "suffer forever, earn more". Tapping out is free and celebrated.
rebuilt.physical_prop: A tray with a Warheads Extreme, a lemon wedge as the backup for judges who won't eat candy, and a full glass of milk sitting on a bright printed coaster with a "DO NOT LIFT" ring. A phone on a small tripod looks down at the tray and the judge's face. A laptop or TV shows the giant ticker, and three teammates' phones show three draining $5 hold bars.
rebuilt.core_loop:
1. Someone posts a dare into the friend group ("Warhead Extreme, 30s, who's backing?").
2. Friends tap "Back it". Each one creates a real capped authorization (a hold, for example $5). Or a standing mandate covers it automatically: "back any dare in Floor 4 up to $3, $15/week, ask me above $5."
3. The challenger shows the item to the camera. OCR confirms it's on the whitelist and allergen-clear, and the clock arms.
4. Item in mouth, and the ticker climbs at pot ÷ 30 per second. Backers' phones show their holds draining live.
5. The glass leaves the coaster (or 30s hits), and the clock freezes.
6. Settlement: each hold is partially captured for (seconds ÷ 30) × stake, the remainder is reversed, and the captured total is pushed to the challenger's card.
7. A 6-second auto-clip of the face-fold moment goes to the group chat with the time stamped ("Anson: 22.0s, $8.80").
8. The friend-group segment board updates ("Floor 4 record, Warhead Extreme: 27.4s").
Repeat Friday. Optional "Sour for a Cause" mode, borrowed from Pledge Plate: the pot pays a club fundraiser or the floor's pizza order instead of the challenger. This is the dining-hall and club-rush version.
rebuilt.demo_script_90s:
0-10s: "Want to make nine dollars in thirty seconds?" Hand the judge the Warhead. The three teammates' phones are already up showing "$5.00 held" each. One teammate says "I'm backing it" and taps, and a fourth hold appears live, so the judge sees real auths land.
10-20s: The judge holds the Warhead to the camera. The overlay reads "WARHEADS EXTREME · sour · no capsaicin · no declared allergens → ARMED". Point at it: "That label check is the safety gate. Pepper challenge chips get refused."
20-45s: It goes in. The TV ticker climbs $0.33... $0.67... and the teammates groan as their bars drain on their phones. The judge's face folds around 15-25s. The glass comes off the coaster, the frame freezes, and a red "MILK BREAK 22.0s" appears.
45-60s: Settlement plays out on screen line by line, using real Cybersource sandbox responses: "Partial capture $2.20 ×4 · Reversal $2.80 ×4 · Push to card $8.80 → judge". Show the clip auto-posted to the mock group chat and the judge's name on the Floor board under the record.
60-90s: The why, in two lines. "Every dorm already does this dare. It breaks down because backers say 'I was joking' and everyone argues about whether it counted. Holds fix the first, the camera fixes the second, and paying by the second makes your own face the price." For a judge who won't eat anything, flip them to the backer role: they back $5 and watch their own hold drain while a teammate eats the lemon. Funnier, and they still touch the demo.
rebuilt.money_moment: The glass leaves the coaster at 22.0 seconds. The ticker freezes at $8.80. On four phones, each backer's bar splits into a captured part (red, $2.20) and a released part (green, $2.80, "reversed"), and $8.80 lands on the judge's card. The judge's own suffering set the price to the cent, and the backers can see exactly what it cost them.
rebuilt.social_layer_decision:
KEEP, but narrowed. All three judges ruled that social helps here, and it does for a structural reason, not a decorative one: the money has to come from other people and the joke needs an audience. With no friends there is no pot and no reason to do it.

What stays: friend-group pots; the clip shared to the group chat (iMessage/GroupMe share, not an in-app public feed); and Strava-style per-food segments scoped to a friend group or floor ("Floor 4 record, Warhead Extreme 27.4s"). Because of the 30s cap, the segment tops out at "beat the clock". The flex is beating it, not enduring longer than anyone has ever endured.

What's cut: any global or public leaderboard, any cross-food aggregate score, and any public feed. The expo-judge flagged that a global endurance board becomes a health-optics problem, and a single number turns a Friday-night bit into a grind.

General rule for the team's question: a social layer helps when it is the money source or the audience the conceit needs. It hurts when it's a score bolted on so there's something to rank (the dead "eating-well points" pattern).
rebuilt.visa_role:
All of these are real sandbox primitives, with no item-level declines and no new cards:
(1) Each backer creates a Cybersource sandbox authorization with capture=false, sized to their stake, expiring at the dare deadline. This is the binding "I wasn't joking."
(2) At settlement, a single partial capture per backer for (seconds survived ÷ 30) × stake, followed by an authorization reversal of the remainder. Be honest with judges: the live ticker shows the pending capture amount, and the actual capture fires once, at the freeze. That's how real partial capture works, and saying so builds trust.
(3) The captured funds go to the challenger via a Visa Direct push-to-card (sandbox), or to the club's card in Sour for a Cause mode.
(4) Recurring backers set a Payment Instructions-style mandate with a per-dare cap, a weekly cap, an expiry, and an approval prompt above a threshold. The app creates holds under the mandate without a tap each time.
(5) Optional small agent feature: a TAP-signed agent checkout restocks the floor's "dare tray" (Warheads, lemons) from the pot's 5% house cut, capped by the same mandate. It's a footnote, not the core.

Framing: the challenger never stakes money, so it's sponsorship of a skill/endurance stunt, not wagering. Backers can't win money, they can only pay less.
rebuilt.trust_story:
Backers: their maximum exposure is the hold they chose, it expires automatically, and whatever isn't earned is reversed. They watch it happen on their own phone.
Challenger: the money is already authorized before the clock starts, so nobody can flake.
Disputes: the 6-second clip and the freeze frame (glass off the coaster) are the ruling. A backer can flag a spit-out within 2 minutes and the group votes on the replay. The camera handles the 95% case and humans handle the edge.
Safety, said out loud at the table: OCR whitelist gate (sour, bitter and weird foods only, no capsaicin products, so it's not One Chip), an allergen check against the ingredient panel, a hard 30s cap, tapping out is always free, a maximum of 3 dares per person per night, and no global records.
Visa optics: no challenger stake means no wager, payouts are capped by mandate, and every movement is a standard auth, capture, reversal or push.
rebuilt.build_36h:
Person A (vision): phone on a tripod streams frames at 3-5 fps to Perceptron Mk1. Three prompts: (a) label and ingredient OCR, mapped to a whitelist and blacklist and an allergen check; (b) grounding the glass bounding box against the printed coaster zone, with "glass displaced more than X% from the coaster for 2 consecutive frames" as the freeze trigger; (c) a mouth/item check at arm time only. A manual "tap out" button is the fallback if vision lags, disclosed rather than hidden.
Person B (payments): Node backend calling Cybersource sandbox REST (auth with capture=false, partial capture, auth reversal) plus Visa Direct sandbox PushFundsTransaction. The two-way SSL cert setup takes about an hour, so do it Friday night. If Visa Direct blocks, keep auth/capture/reversal real and label the push "sandbox pending". Mandate object: caps, expiry and approval threshold enforced server-side before holds are created.
Person C (realtime frontend): web app (no App Store needed). Big ticker view for the TV; backer phone view with draining bars over websockets; dare creation and "Back it" flow; clip capture (ring buffer, last 6s exported to MP4 on freeze).
Person D (social and polish): group chat share sheet, Floor segment board, Sour for a Cause toggle, the printed coaster, tray staging, and buying a box of Warheads, lemons and milk. D owns the 90-second script and rehearses with strangers.
Milestones: Sat noon, real auth plus reversal end to end. Sat 6pm, glass-off-coaster trigger reliable under expo lighting. Sat midnight, full loop. Sun morning, rehearsal only.
rebuilt.fatal_flaw:
Not fatal, but there are three real risks, in order.
(1) Prior art. Cash-backed dare apps exist (Double Dog, Monster Dare, Bounty won in 2026). The defense only works if the per-second, two-sided live meter is the first thing judges see. If the team leads with "friends escrow money for dares," it dies as "Bounty again". Never say "escrow" in the first 30 seconds.
(2) Safety optics with Visa judges. Even with sour-only items, some judges will flinch at "get paid to suffer." The OCR safety gate, the 30s cap and the Sour for a Cause mode have to be spoken out loud, not buried. If a judge still recoils, switch them to the backer role.
(3) Live-meter honesty. If a judge asks "is it actually capturing every second?", the answer is no: one partial capture at the freeze, with the ticker showing the pending amount. Say that confidently rather than overclaiming.
A softer risk: hygiene and willingness at an expo table. Bring individually wrapped candies, lemon wedges in cups, a fresh glass per judge, and the backer-role alternative.

rebuilt.name: Toppled (the snack tower decides who pays for the snacks)
rebuilt.pitch_10s: Stack the party snacks into one tower. Whoever knocks it over pays for every snack in the tower, and everyone else splits whatever is still on the tray. The camera prices the tower live as it grows, and the host is paid back the moment it hits the table.
rebuilt.the_new_thing:
The groceries are the game pieces, the scoreboard and the bill all at once. A phone on a tripod watches a tray. Perceptron reads each snack's label to identify the product (Takis Fuego, Shin Ramyun cup, Oreo sleeve) and looks up its price in the host's snack list. The host builds that list in the app before the party by scanning each item's label once at setup, so there is no receipt splitting. A snack only counts as placed after it has stood still on the tower for 3 seconds with no hand in frame. The 3-second rule is borrowed from Toppler. When it counts, the big 'TOWER $' number climbs. A collapse is a detected event: the tracked item boxes lose most of the tower's height, or several items move from their last stable positions within half a second. Turn order comes from the app (your phone buzzes 'your move'), so the camera never has to guess whose hand it was. That claim is cut.

The rule changes from 'loser pays a growing number' to a fixed-bill split. The total money moved is exactly what the host spent on snacks, never a cent more. The only thing the game decides is who pays which part. Every snack you place moves its price out of the shared pool, where you would owe a share, and onto the tower, where only the toppler pays. So building lowers your own expected bill but makes the tower scarier for the next player. That is the push-your-luck mechanic the cynical-student liked in Toppler, kept here with real groceries instead of identical cans.
rebuilt.physical_prop: A tray with a pre-built half tower plus a side pile of real snacks with awkward shapes: Shin Ramyun cups, a Cheez-It box, an Oreo sleeve, a Pocky box, two cans, a Takis bag and a Pringles tube. The demo set is curated, so roughly 70% of the shapes stack well and the bag and tube are the risky picks. The judge picks a snack and balances it on the tower. Behind the tray, a TV or laptop shows the live tower price, each player's tile and the slow-motion replay. A second tray is pre-stacked so the next judge never waits for a rebuild.
rebuilt.core_loop:
1. Host setup, done once: scan each snack's label to build the snack list (for example $30.00 total) and pick a cap (default $20).
2. Join: each guest taps their phone and approves a $20 hold. Their tile shows 'HOLD $20 - worst case'.
3. Turns: on your turn you pick a snack from the tray and place it on the tower. After 3 seconds standing, the label is read, its price moves from the shared pool to TOWER $, and the screen flashes '+$4.49 Takis'.
4. Collapse: the camera detects the fall. The person whose turn it was is the toppler, and only snacks that had already counted as placed are included in the tower.
5. Settle: the toppler's hold is partly captured for TOWER $, capped at the hold. The remaining bill (snacks still on the tray) is split evenly among the other players, and each of their holds is partly captured for that share. The leftover on every hold is released. The host's own share is netted out, and the host gets one push payout for everyone else's money.
6. Everyone eats the wreckage. If the tray empties without a collapse, the tower stood: the bill is split evenly, and the tower goes on the house record wall.
rebuilt.demo_script_90s:
0-10s: A teammate hands the judge a phone with a sandbox card loaded: 'Tap to join. That's a $20 hold. It's the most this can ever cost you.' The judge's tile appears on the TV next to three teammates (one is the host, Sam). Header: 'Snacks bill $30.00 | TOWER $9.47'.
10-20s: The rule, said once: 'Whatever's in the tower, the toppler pays. Whatever's still on the tray, everyone else splits.'
20-35s: The judge balances a Takis bag on the half tower. After 3 seconds the label gets a bounding box, '+$4.49 Takis Fuego' flashes, and TOWER $ goes to $13.96. The shared pool drops on everyone's tile.
35-45s: A teammate adds an Oreo sleeve: '+$2.99', TOWER $16.95. The tower leans. The teammate says to the judge, 'Your move.'
45-60s: The judge places a ramen cup and the tower falls (if it doesn't, a teammate goes next and knocks it over on purpose). The camera catches the collapse with no button press. The TV plays a 2-second slow-motion replay stamped 'TOPPLED - $16.95 - JUDGE'.
60-75s: All four phones buzz together. Judge: '$16.95 captured, $3.05 released.' The two other teammates: '$4.35 captured, $15.65 released.' Sam (host): 'Your share $4.35 netted, $25.65 pushed to your card.' A breakdown appears under the tiles: 16.95 + 3 x 4.35 = $30.00, the exact snack bill.
75-90s: Close: 'Every dollar that moved is the host's snack money, and nobody received a cent except the person who paid for the food. The cap was the promise. That's real Cybersource auths, partial captures and a Visa Direct push, no mocks.' Hand the judge a Pocky from the wreckage.
rebuilt.money_moment: The snacks hit the table, the slow-motion replay plays with 'TOPPLED - $16.95 - JUDGE' stamped over it, and four phones buzz at the same moment, each with a different exact number. It is Minty's structure: the money is the punchline of a physical slapstick moment. The fixed-bill rule makes it funnier rather than meaner, because the judge watched $7.48 of snacks go onto the tower that they would have split four ways if they had left it alone. The second beat is the trust beat: the five numbers on screen add up to exactly $30.00.
rebuilt.social_layer_decision: KEEP the in-room social core, CUT any feed or leaderboard, and KEEP the replay wall, adding one cooperative record. The game has no solo version, so the people in the room are the product. That answers 'should we add a social layer' for this idea: it already is one. All three judges agreed that a cross-group 'who paid most' ranking turns a party bit into a shame chart, and a Strava feed of strangers' snack towers adds nothing. I'm cutting both. What stays is the replay wall of collapse clips (most expensive topple, funniest fall), which people share as videos. That is the viral surface, and it carries no points. The one goal score worth adding is a cooperative house record, 'tallest tower that ever stood: $41.20 (Oct 17)'. It belongs to the apartment, not to a person, so it pushes everyone to build higher, which raises the stakes for whoever is next. That tension is the fun. Nobody gets an individual lifetime stat.
rebuilt.visa_role:
These are real sandbox operations, and the story is now N different partial captures, not 'one capture and N voids'.
(1) Join: Cybersource sandbox authorization of $20 per player, the consented cap.
(2) Settle: partial capture for every player, each a different amount (the toppler's tower value, the others' split of the tray), and the remaining authorization is released (reversal of the unused amount). If the bill is fully covered before someone's share comes up, for example because the host's own share nets to zero, that player's hold is voided outright.
(3) Host payout: one Visa Direct push-funds (OCT) sandbox call to the host's own card for the bill minus the host's own share. No new cards are issued to anyone.
(4) Night mandate, Payment Instructions-style: 'Toppled at Sam's: up to $40 across games, expires 2:00am'. A new round's hold above the mandate triggers an approval prompt on the player's phone, and at expiry the stored token is suspended automatically, so nobody's card stays armed after the party.
The cap, the exact-sum settlement and the auto-suspend are the Visa pitch: programmable consent that makes a 'loser buys' house rule safe to automate. No item-level declines and no fake issuing.
rebuilt.trust_story:
Three promises, all enforced by the payment rails rather than by the app's goodwill:
(a) The cap: the worst case is the $20 you approved, and a collapse can't cost more, even if the tower is worth $35. Any overflow is split evenly among the others.
(b) The fixed bill: the total captured always equals exactly the host's snack list. There is no pot, no winner payout and no house cut, and the only person who receives money is the one who bought the food. This is the answer to the gambling-optics objection. It isn't a bet, because nobody can come out ahead. It's a split rule decided by a dexterity game instead of a calculator. Say 'loser buys the snacks', never 'credit card roulette'.
(c) The tape: every settlement comes with the replay clip and the per-snack placement log (who placed what, at what price), so a disputed topple can be watched back. Any player can tap 'contest' within 60 seconds, which voids that round and splits it evenly. Everyone sees the snack list prices before joining, and the night's token is suspended at expiry.
rebuilt.build_36h:
Person A (vision): Perceptron on a 3-5 fps stream from the tripod phone. Use label OCR or grounding to match items against a 15-20 SKU snack list built from one label scan per item at setup. Tracking state machine: in-hand, then stable for 3 seconds, then placed. Collapse detector: tower bounding-box height drops by more than 50%, or 3 or more placed items move by more than X px within 500ms. Keep a 5-second frame ring buffer and export a slow-motion replay with ffmpeg.
Person B (game backend): Node/FastAPI with WebSocket state: players, turn order, shared pool, TOWER $, the settle math (cap overflow, host netting, exact-sum check) and the contest window.
