Person C (payments): Cybersource sandbox auth, partial capture, reversal/void and token management. Visa Direct push-funds sandbox call. Mandate object with cap, expiry and an approval-prompt webhook to the phone.
Person D (front end and stage): a TV view (big TOWER $ number, player tiles, replay stamp) and a mobile join/approve page (PWA, not a native app). Curate the demo snack set, test 30+ real collapses on the expo table under that lighting, and pre-stack two trays.
Hour 30 freeze. Fallbacks: a hidden 'collapse' key if vision misses a fall; a can-only tower (Toppler) if label reads are flaky on bags; a pre-recorded replay if ffmpeg is slow. Cut list: agent restock, cross-device clip sharing.
rebuilt.fatal_flaw: Not fatal, but these are the residual risks hostile judges will push on. (1) Gambling optics at a Visa booth: the fixed-bill, no-winner rule plus the cap defuses most of it, but only if the team never says 'roulette' or 'bet', and the on-screen sum check has to be the closing line every time. (2) Physical reliability: placement and collapse detection on bags and tubes at a noisy, badly lit expo is the most likely way this fails live. That is why the snack set is curated, the 3-second stability rule is in, the can fallback exists, and there is a hidden override key. Test on the actual table, not a dorm desk. (3) Overlap with Toppler: ship this one, not both. This version wins because the snacks are the bill, which makes it a grocery idea rather than Jenga with a price tag. (4) A 'loser buys' rule on real money among close friends could feel petty. The answer is the low cap, the contest-and-split-evenly button, and the fact that the stakes are a few dollars of chips the toppler eats too.

verdicts.name: Toppled (the snack tower decides who pays for the snacks)
verdicts.killer_argument: Most damaging: soft snacks don't make a real tower. Takis bags, Pringles tubes and Oreo sleeves give you a slumped pile of 5 or 6 items, not a Jenga moment. The collapse also comes after maybe 4 placements, so the 'push your luck' tension is shorter than the rule explanation. If the curated set leans on cans and boxes to stay stackable, it turns into 'Jenga with a price tag', and the grocery connection (the label OCR) starts to look like decoration. A second risk is that 'loser pays more than half the party bill' is exactly the petty-among-friends feeling round 1 killed in pay-per-slice. Two things save it. First, credit-card roulette is a real ritual students already play unprompted, so this passes the Friday-night test. Second, the slapstick fall is a perfect Minty-style punchline. It survives because the judge is physically the actor, the money result is instant and funny, and the vision has three real jobs that a button can't fake: identify the SKU from the label, confirm the item stood still for 3 seconds, and detect the collapse.
verdicts.prior_art: Searches found no camera-detected-collapse payment game and no Devpost project combining stacking with loser-pays. The physical mechanic is old: Jenga, Ravensburger MazePop and tumble towers all use 'the player who topples it loses'. Digital stacking apps (Topple Tower on Vision Pro, Stacks Tower) have no real-world camera and no payments. Credit-card roulette is the real-world precedent for letting chance decide who pays, which is both its strongest validation and its gambling-optics liability. The team's own earlier 'Toppler' (cans) is the closest relative, so ship this version only.
verdicts.social_layer_ruling: The in-room social layer is the product, because the game has no solo version and should not have one. Cut every feed and every individual or cross-group 'who paid most' board. That is a shame chart, and it's what turns a party bit into a debt ledger. The replay clip as a shareable video is fine, because it's the natural viral surface and it isn't a score. The cooperative 'tallest tower that ever stood' house record is harmless but worth zero rubric points. Keep it off the demo screen and spend those 5 seconds on the sum-check closing line.
verdicts.what_would_make_it_great: (1) Make the stack physically interesting. Use a 'base tray plus snacks' rule that lets the judge put a bag on a can tower, and show the price-per-height tradeoff (a cheap Pocky box is safe, a $4.49 Takis bag is risky and expensive). Then placement becomes a visible money decision and not just a balance check. (2) Cap the toppler at a smaller share, for example the tower value or 50% of the bill, whichever is lower, so the hit stings without feeling punitive. (3) Make the on-screen 16.95 + 3 x 4.35 = 30.00 the final frame every time. (4) Lean on the night-mandate token-suspend-at-2am for the Visa judge. It's the one primitive in this batch that the other two don't use, and it answers 'why Visa and not Venmo'. (5) Test 30+ collapses on a folding table under bad fluorescent light before the event, with a hidden collapse key as backup.

verdicts.name: Cleaned Out: Loser Buys the Groceries
verdicts.killer_argument: The 'vote' measures flavor and placement, not cooking. Chocolate chip beats matcha on any plate, at any table, every time, so the money ends up punishing whoever drew the weird flavor, and 'eating is the vote' becomes 'the safest cookie wins'. That is an unfair verdict with real money attached. A Visa judge will also need about 30 of their 180 seconds to follow the settlement: losers' leftover amounts scaled to fit under the winner's self-declared ingredient cost, plus an honor-system cost field. A second weakness is that the judge has no money at stake. Their bite moves a stranger's hold. That's a nice beat, but weaker than Toppled, where the judge pays. It still survives on four points: the bite-to-bar-drain moment really does mirror Minty, cookie counting is the kind of task Perceptron is genuinely good at, 'CHEF HAND, doesn't count' is a real laugh, and the guest does nothing but eat.
verdicts.prior_art: No app or hack was found that uses how fast a dish empties as the cook-off ballot. Potluck and cook-off judging is always panels, secret ballots or public votes (Folly Beach cook-off, university potlucks, MangoApps recipe-contest templates). The only match is an office-potluck anecdote about bragging rights over which dish disappeared fastest, which suggests the behavior is real but has no tool behind it. Plate-waste cameras (Winnow, Leanpath) are back-of-house analytics, not ballots.
verdicts.social_layer_ruling: Rival chefs in one room are the mechanism, so that layer has to stay. Cut the Floor 4 League and the personal-best clear times from the pitch. That's the Strava-lite layer, and no judge can verify 'people come back weekly' in 3 minutes. It also invites the question of why a league needs money at all. Keep only the optional timelapse clip of the winning plate emptying, for the group chat.
verdicts.what_would_make_it_great: (1) Remove the flavor bias. Make it a same-recipe bake-off (everyone makes chocolate chip) or a blind tasting where plates are swapped by color at halftime, so the eat rate actually measures skill. (2) Simplify the settlement to one sentence: 'losers split the winner's grocery receipt in proportion to their leftovers.' Drop the scaling explanation from the spoken pitch. (3) Give the judge skin in the game: the judge registers as a fourth 'chef' with a pre-made plate, or the judge's bite 'saves' a chef they choose. (4) It works for dumplings or wings at a real floor event. Pick the countable food that Perceptron counts most reliably under clutter, and run the demo on that.

verdicts.name: Sour Clock
verdicts.killer_argument: The camera is a stopwatch with extra steps. The event that moves money is a milk glass leaving a coaster, which is a tap-out button with a computer-vision costume. The thing that makes the dare funny, the judge's face folding, is something the system explicitly does not measure. The label-OCR 'safety gate' is a job invented to justify the vision model, and an expo judge will notice. Once the camera is stripped out, what's left is friends pre-funding a dare and the challenger getting paid on completion, with a time multiplier. That's Double Dog, Monster Dare, iNominate and Bounty (a 2026 hackathon winner, escrow-on-proof), and the Visa flow is the same auth/partial-capture/reverse/push choreography. Two more problems sink it at the booth. A Visa brand judge will flinch at 'get paid to suffer' food challenges no matter how many safety caveats are spoken. And many judges will not put an unwrapped stranger's candy or lemon in their mouth at an expo, so the 'judge as actor' opener falls back to the weaker backer role.
verdicts.prior_art: Double Dog (2016, cash dares with video proof), Monster Dare (wager money on dares, 10% fee), Klash (2012), iNominate (24-hour cash challenges), Sable (on-chain USDC-locked challenges), and Bounty (2026 hackathon winner, escrow released on proof). The Warheads or sour-candy endurance challenge itself is a long-running viral meme, so the behavior is real. But the monetized-dare app category is crowded and has historically closed down on safety and fee complaints.
verdicts.social_layer_ruling: The friend pot is structurally needed, since the money must come from other people. If it survived, the group-chat clip would be the right share surface. The per-food segment board ('Floor 4 record, Warhead Extreme 27.4s') should not exist even scoped to a floor. It is literally an endurance leaderboard for eating something painful, which is the exact health-optics trap the expo judge flagged, and a 30s cap only means everyone ties at the top.
verdicts.what_would_make_it_great: It would need the camera to see the thing that matters: the price comes from what Perceptron sees on the face or body (pucker, wince, hand reaching), not from a coaster. Even then, it competes in the same 'loser pays / proof-of-act' slot as Toppled, with worse Visa optics. Recommendation: fold its one good idea, a live per-second meter where backers watch their holds drain on their own phones, into Toppled or Cleaned Out. Don't build it.

ranking: Toppled (the snack tower decides who pays for the snacks)
Cleaned Out: Loser Buys the Groceries
execution.batch_diagnosis:
Two of the three survive. Toppled is ahead because it is the only one where the judge physically acts, the judge's own money moves, and the vision model has jobs that a button can't fake: reading the SKU label, checking the item stood still for 3 seconds, and detecting the collapse. Cleaned Out is a solid second, but its vote measures flavor popularity more than cooking, and its settlement math eats demo time. Sour Clock dies because its camera is a disguised tap-out button and it sits directly in the Double Dog / Monster Dare / Bounty category.

On the team's social question, the batch gives a clean answer. All three finalists independently reached the same rule, and the evidence supports it. A social or competition layer improves an idea only when the other people are physically present AND are the source of the money. In that case it isn't a 'layer' at all, it's the mechanism: rival plates, tower players, backers. Anything added asynchronously on top makes the idea worse: Strava-style feeds, leagues, personal bests, cross-group leaderboards, goal scores. There are three reasons. A judge can't experience it in 3 minutes, so it scores zero on Functionality and Design. It is what round 1 already killed (eating-well points, adherence scores). And once real money is involved, a ranking turns into either a betting board or a shame chart, and Visa judges will mark both down. So the answer to 'should we add a Strava or competition aspect' is no as an add-on, and yes only if the idea is a multiplayer game in the room from the start. Don't put a goal score on a solo action.

On the hostile-agent framing: no adversarial agent is needed. The natural 'opponents' here are the other people at the table, and that is more fun and easier to demo than a synthetic adversary.

On the grocery-list card worry: Toppled's per-item label read is a genuine vision job (dense-label OCR to identify the SKU), not a paper-card clone. Keep paper cards, projectors and handwritten inputs out of every demo, so no judge can say 'Math Sandbox again'.

There is a batch-level warning. All three finalists converge on the same template: a party game where the loser pays, settled as amount-capped auth → partial capture → reversal → Visa Direct push. That monoculture brings two risks. Every 'loser pays' framing invites gambling-optics questions at a Visa booth, so lead with the fixed-bill, no-one-profits sum check. And the Visa story starts to look like a reusable settlement widget, not something the idea needs. Toppled escapes this best because its night mandate with automatic token suspension at expiry gives a distinct reason why programmable Visa consent matters and Venmo-after-the-fact doesn't.

Infrastructure note: Visa Direct sandbox requires two-way SSL with a Visa-issued X.509 certificate from the project dashboard, so the Friday-night cert setup in the build plans is mandatory.
